items.fromString:
Today Cost Management can process OpenShift data and cloud data.

OpenShift data is posted by customers to the API, i. e. customer-initiated and we do not connect to their OpenShift cluster, or even touch their network.

Cloud data, on the other hand, is Red Hat-initiated: customers write (automatically or on their own) Cost and Usage Reports (or equivalent) into a storage bucket and Cost Management connects to the customer’s bucket to download the data. This requires that customers allow Cost Management to connect to their buckets, which typically requires clearance from IT Security departments.

This feature request is about providing a way for customers to send their data via the Cost Management API, same as OpenShift data can be sent. This way, Cost Management will not connect to the customer bucket, hence no IT Security concerns.

Since we will need a mechanism for customers to upload FOCUS data to Cost Management, and the three major hyperscalers support FOCUS data export, my suggestion is we will only implement this “cloud data via Cost Management API” to FOCUS data. AWS CUR and equivalent native billing data stay Red Hat-initiated download from user bucket, unless there’s technical reasons to go in a different direction.

items.fromString:
*Goal*

A complete solution for lifecycle of price lists

*User stories*

* As a admin, I want to be able to define different versions of the price model, so that the proper version can be shown for stored and new calculation

* As an admin, I want to be able to define when a new version will be applied

*Problem*

Being able to differentiate between charges being calculated and recalculated for the current billing period with the charges that were calculated in the past with a different price model.

*Why is this important*

It allows admins to manage their price models and enable new versions in advance, so they can set them up without waiting for the billing period when they want it be applied to be active.

*Examples*

Example 1.

A user looks at the data for 3 months ago. The price model has been changed since that moment and there is new active one, but the calculations where done with an old version of it.

When the user sees any calculated data in the interface he is presented with the version of the price model that was used to calculate the data, and a message that lets him know if there is a new version of the cost model.

Example 2.

An admin knows that they want to change the markup on a cloud with the new year, from 10% to 20%. The administrator decides to implement the price model modification today, but with an applicability date of the new year. During the months until the price model change, the current model is used, and the admin can update the price model without creating a new version.

Once the date is reached, the new model is used.

Example 3

AWS updates its price list, and calculations are updated. As there are no changes in the price model, the user still sees the same model

items.fromString:
h2. Summary

Two related issues found during QE validation of [FLPATH-4136|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/FLPATH-4136] (AWS S3 support):

h3. Issue 1: Hardcoded addressing_style in ConfigMap

{{configmap-aws-config.yaml}} hardcodes {{addressing_style = path}}. AWS S3 requires {{auto}} (virtual-hosted style) for non-us-east-1 regions and dot-containing bucket names. The value needs to be parameterized through {{values.yaml}} and templated in the ConfigMap.

h3. Issue 2: Install script doesn't pass addressingStyle to Helm

{{install-helm-chart.sh}} {{deploy_helm_chart()}} never passes {{objectStorage.s3.addressingStyle}} to Helm. The script already detects AWS endpoints (via {{is_aws_s3_endpoint_host()}}) for bucket creation but doesn't carry that through to chart values.

h2. Impact

Any AWS S3 deployment outside us-east-1 or with dots in the bucket name will fail with S3 addressing errors. Koku and ingress pods always receive {{addressing_style = path}} regardless of backend type.

h2. Fix

* Add {{addressingStyle: "path"}} to {{values.yaml}} under {{objectStorage.s3}} (default preserves backward compat)
* Template the value in {{_helpers.tpl}} and {{configmap-aws-config.yaml}}
* Have {{deploy_helm_chart()}} pass {{--set objectStorage.s3.addressingStyle=auto}} when it detects an AWS endpoint

h2. Version Info

Found on branch {{flpath-4136-qe-aws-s3-helm-support}} at commit {{761e3b2}}
items.toString:
h2. Summary

Two related issues found during QE validation of [FLPATH-4136|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/FLPATH-4136] (AWS S3 support):

h3. Issue 1: Hardcoded addressing_style in ConfigMap

{{configmap-aws-config.yaml}} hardcodes {{addressing_style = path}} as a raw string literal. In contrast, {{region}} on the same file is properly templated via {{cost-onprem.storage.s3Region}}. Every pod that mounts this ConfigMap (Koku, MASU, ingress, celery workers, listener) is locked to path-style addressing with no way to override it without forking the chart.

h3. Issue 2: Install script doesn't pass addressingStyle to Helm

{{install-helm-chart.sh}} {{deploy_helm_chart()}} never passes {{objectStorage.s3.addressingStyle}} to Helm. The script already detects AWS endpoints via {{is_aws_s3_endpoint_host()}} and correctly sets {{addressing_style=auto}} for the ephemeral bucket-creation job, but does not carry that through to the chart values that govern the long-lived application pods.

h2. Impact & Severity

*Severity: Medium (future-proofing, not current breakage)*

Path-style S3 addressing still works today on AWS S3 in all regions. AWS announced deprecation of path-style access in 2019, but *indefinitely delayed enforcement* and has not set a new date. However:

* The hardcoded value overrides boto3's default behavior ({{auto}}), which intelligently selects the right addressing style per-bucket
* When AWS eventually enforces the deprecation, every pod consuming this ConfigMap will fail against AWS S3
* There is no way for a customer to change the addressing style without forking the chart
* For on-prem backends (NooBaa, Ceph RGW, S4, MinIO), {{path}} is correct — these backends generally do not support virtual-hosted style

h2. Background: S3 Addressing Styles

*Path-style* puts the bucket name in the URL path: {{https://s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/my-bucket/object}}

*Virtual-hosted style* puts the bucket name in the hostname: {{https://my-bucket.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/object}}

{{auto}} (boto3 default) uses virtual-hosted style but falls back to path-style for edge cases (e.g., bucket names containing dots, which break TLS wildcard cert matching).

h2. AWS Deprecation References

* [Amazon S3 Path Deprecation Plan — The Rest of the Story|https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/amazon-s3-path-deprecation-plan-the-rest-of-the-story/] (AWS Blog, Sep 2019): Original enforcement date of Sep 30, 2020 was indefinitely postponed.
* [Virtual hosting of buckets|https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/VirtualHosting.html] (AWS Docs): Documents that virtual-hosted style is the preferred method and that path-style will eventually be discontinued for new buckets.
* boto3 defaults to {{auto}} when no {{addressing_style}} is configured. The {{auto}} setting lets the SDK pick virtual-hosted or path-style per-request based on bucket name characteristics.

h2. Fix

# Add {{addressingStyle: "path"}} to {{values.yaml}} under {{objectStorage.s3}} (default preserves backward compat for on-prem backends)
# Template the value in {{_helpers.tpl}} (following existing {{s3Region}} pattern) and {{configmap-aws-config.yaml}}
# Have {{deploy_helm_chart()}} pass {{--set objectStorage.s3.addressingStyle=auto}} when it detects an AWS endpoint (using existing {{is_aws_s3_endpoint_host()}})

h2. Version Info

Found on branch {{flpath-4136-qe-aws-s3-helm-support}} at commit {{761e3b2}}

items.fromString:
Building a temporary containerized version of the RBAC UI to test end-to-end integration against Jordi's recent Helm chart PR. This will validate the deployment flow and custom configurations before the upcoming sync with the RBAC UI team.

h3. *Scope of Work*

* *Build:* Package the RBAC UI "as-is," ensuring components flagged by Stefan for removal are excluded at this point.
* *Configure:* Apply custom settings required for *on-prem* environments.
* *Containerize:* Use a standard {{nginx}} base image to host the build.
* *Registry:* Push the resulting image to a personal Quay organization for testing.
* *Validation:* Update the Helm chart in the local environment (layered on top of Jordi's PR) to point to the new image and verify the UI loads and communicates correctly.

h3. *Acceptance Criteria*

* RBAC UI successfully builds with on-premise configurations.
* Docker image is available in Quay.
* Deployment to the cluster (via Helm chart modifications) is successful.
* Basic connectivity/integration with Jordi's changes is verified.
items.toString:
h3. Goal
Deliver _insights\-rbac\-ui_ as a *micro\-frontend \(MFE\)* inside the existing on\-prem Cost shell \(*koku\-ui\-onprem*\), aligned with parent *FLPATH\-3424* — not a separate “sibling” app, extra OpenShift UI Route, or standalone nginx\-only deployment as the primary delivery path.

h3. Context
* The on\-prem host \({{apps/koku\-ui\-onprem}}\) already loads federated modules via *Scalprum* \+ *ModuleFederationPlugin*; remotes use *DynamicRemotePlugin* \(same pattern as *koku\-ui\-hccm* → scope {{costManagement}}, plus *koku\-ui\-ros*, *koku\-ui\-sources*\).
* *cost\-onprem\-chart* exposes the RBAC admin API at gateway path *{{/api/rbac/}}* \(Envoy → insights\-rbac\). Browser calls should use the *same origin* as the UI so JWT and *X\-Rh\-Identity* behavior matches cluster deployment.
* Stakeholder direction: same Keycloak realm as *cost\-management\-ui*; RBAC API delivered by the chart \(*FLPATH\-4073* / insights\-rbac backend\).

h3. Scope of work
* *Build \(remote\):* Add an on\-prem webpack build for *insights\-rbac\-ui* using *DynamicRemotePlugin*: choose {{pluginMetadata.name}}, {{publicPath}} \(e.g. {{/rbac/}}\), expose a root module \(e.g. {{./RootApp}}\) with an entry wrapper \(Intl / Redux / notifications as required by upstream\).
* *Shims:* Extend {{libs/onprem\-cloud\-deps}} and webpack {{resolve.alias}} so SaaS\-only imports \({{@redhat\-cloud\-services/\*}}, Unleash, chrome\) resolve on\-prem; extend {{window.insights.chrome}} stubs in the host if RBAC UI needs APIs beyond what HCCM needs.
* *Host integration:* In *koku\-ui\-onprem*: register the remote in *ScalprumProvider* \({{manifestLocation}} under the chosen {{publicPath}}\); add *Route\(s\)* \+ *ScalprumComponent* \+ nav; add {{devServer.static}} for the remote {{dist}} in local dev; add {{devServer.proxy}} for *{{/api/rbac}}* \(today only {{/api/cost\-management/v1}} is proxied\).
* *Monorepo:* Wire the package into root *{{build:onprem}}* / *{{start:onprem}}* \({{concurrently}}\) so CI and local workflows build the RBAC remote before the host.
* *Validation:* Prove the RBAC MFE loads in the shell and performs IAM operations against *{{/api/rbac/}}* on a cluster with the current chart \(*no second UI hostname* required for acceptance\).

h3. Out of scope / deprecated for this ticket
* *Standalone nginx image \+ separate Helm image ref* as the _primary_ delivery \(optional throwaway smoke image only if explicitly needed — not the acceptance target\).
* “Personal Quay org” is *optional* unless we keep a temporary published image for CI; production path is the *existing Cost UI container* serving the host app plus *{{/rbac/}}* \(or chosen path\) static assets.

h3. Acceptance criteria
* RBAC UI builds as a *federated remote* with on\-prem webpack config; produces *{{plugin\-manifest.json}}* \+ chunks under a fixed *{{publicPath}}*.
* *koku\-ui\-onprem* loads the module via *Scalprum* on an agreed route; entry is reachable from the shell.
* *E2E:* Authenticated user can complete RBAC IAM flows against *{{/api/rbac/}}* through the gateway \(same origin as Cost UI\).
* *{{build:onprem}}* \(or documented CI equivalent\) includes the RBAC remote so the integration does not regress.

h3. Notes
* Reconcile “components flagged by Stefan for removal” with *FLPATH\-3424* / *FLPATH\-4121* \(parent stream may assume full POC surface until UX narrows\).
* Upstream contribution model \(build\-time gates vs fork\): *FLPATH\-4152*.

Extract the bundled infrastructure components \(PostgreSQL, Valkey, Kafka/Strimzi setup\) from the cost\-onprem chart into a dedicated infrastructure Helm chart for dev/demo deployments.

This follows the team consensus on [PR #99|https://github.com/insights\-onprem/cost\-onprem\-chart/pull/99|FLPATH-2685] that production deployments should use BYOI exclusively, while dev/demo environments use a two\-chart installation flow:

# Install _infra\-chart_ \(PostgreSQL, Valkey, Kafka\) \-\- dev/demo only
# Install _cost\-onprem\-chart_ \(the application\)

In production, only the second chart is installed. The customer provides their own PostgreSQL, Valkey/Redis, and Kafka endpoints via BYOI configuration \({{database.deploy: false}}, {{valkey.deploy: false}}, {{kafka.bootstrapServers}}\).

h3. Task 1: Create the infrastructure Helm chart

Create a new Helm chart \(e.g. {{cost\-onprem\-infra/}}\) containing the resources currently bundled in the cost\-onprem chart:

* _PostgreSQL StatefulSet_ \-\- from {{cost\-onprem/templates/infrastructure/database/}} \(StatefulSet, Service, init ConfigMap\)
* _Valkey Deployment_ \-\- from {{cost\-onprem/templates/infrastructure/cache/}} \(Deployment, Service, PVC\)
* _Kafka/Strimzi resources_ \-\- currently managed by {{install\-helm\-chart.sh}} \(Strimzi operator subscription, KafkaCluster CR, topic CRs\). Move these into chart templates with appropriate wait/readiness logic.

The infra chart should:
\- Accept a values.yaml that controls which components to deploy \(e.g. {{postgresql.enabled}}, {{valkey.enabled}}, {{kafka.enabled}}\)
\- Expose connection details \(hostnames, ports\) either as output values or via a predictable naming convention that the cost\-onprem chart can reference
\- Create the database credentials secret \(currently done by {{install\-helm\-chart.sh}} via {{create\_database\_credentials\_secret\(\)}}\)
\- Run the PostgreSQL init scripts \(database/user creation\) currently in {{configmap\-init.yaml}}

h3. Task 2: Remove bundled infrastructure from cost\-onprem chart

Once the infra chart exists:
\- Remove the database templates \({{infrastructure/database/}}\) from cost\-onprem
\- Remove the Valkey templates \({{infrastructure/cache/}}\) from cost\-onprem
\- Set {{database.deploy}} and {{valkey.deploy}} defaults to {{false}} in {{values.yaml}} \(BYOI becomes the default\)
\- Keep the BYOI configuration keys \({{database.server.host}}, {{valkey.host}}, {{kafka.bootstrapServers}}\) as the primary connection mechanism
\- Verify {{helm template}} and {{helm lint}} pass with default values \(no bundled infra\)

h3. Task 3: Update install\-helm\-chart.sh

Modify the install script to orchestrate both charts:
\- Install the infra chart first \(into the same namespace or a dedicated infra namespace\)
\- Wait for infrastructure readiness \(PostgreSQL accepting connections, Valkey ready, Kafka topics created\)
\- Derive the BYOI connection values from the infra chart's deployed services
\- Pass those values to the cost\-onprem chart install \(via {{\-\-set}} or a generated values overlay\)
\- Move the database credential creation logic from the script into the infra chart
\- Move the Strimzi/Kafka deployment logic from the script into the infra chart

h3. Task 4: Make BYOI the default CI test mode

* Update the CI test pipeline to deploy infrastructure via the infra chart \(or pre\-existing external services\) rather than relying on bundled infrastructure
* The cost\-onprem chart is installed in BYOI mode, pointing to the infra chart's services
* This validates the production\-like deployment path on every PR
* Bundled\-mode testing \(single chart with everything\) is retired from CI but can still run locally

h3. Task 5: Update documentation

* _Installation guide_: Document the two\-chart flow for dev/demo \(install infra\-chart, then cost\-onprem\-chart\)
* _Production section_: Expand the BYOI section as the primary/recommended installation path
* _Install script reference_: Document the new script behavior \(two\-chart orchestration\)
* _Migration notes_: Document how existing single\-chart deployments can transition to the two\-chart model

h3. Acceptance Criteria

* A standalone infra chart deploys PostgreSQL, Valkey, and Kafka with a single {{helm install}}
* The cost\-onprem chart installs successfully without any bundled infrastructure \(BYOI\-only by default\)
* {{install\-helm\-chart.sh}} installs both charts end\-to\-end for dev/demo setups
* CI runs E2E tests in BYOI mode against infra\-chart\-deployed services
* Documentation clearly describes both installation paths
* No regression in application functionality compared to the current single\-chart approach

h2. Summary

Extract bundled infrastructure components (PostgreSQL StatefulSet, Valkey Deployment) from the cost-onprem Helm chart into conditional Helm subcharts, achieving architectural separation while preserving single-release operational simplicity.

h2. Approach: Conditional Helm Subcharts

After evaluating alternatives (separate standalone chart, Bitnami community charts, keep-and-harden, operator-based), the team selected Helm subcharts with conditional dependencies.

{code:yaml}
dependencies:
  - name: cost-onprem-database
    version: "0.1.0"
    repository: "file://charts/cost-onprem-database"
    condition: database.deploy
  - name: cost-onprem-cache
    version: "0.1.0"
    repository: "file://charts/cost-onprem-cache"
    condition: valkey.deploy
{code}

h2. Scope

*In scope:*
* PostgreSQL -> {{cost-onprem-database}} subchart (conditional on {{database.deploy}})
* Valkey -> {{cost-onprem-cache}} subchart (conditional on {{valkey.deploy}})
* Default: {{database.deploy=false}} (BYOI), {{valkey.deploy=true}} (bundled cache)

*Out of scope:*
* Kafka -- remains in {{deploy-kafka.sh}} (operator prerequisite is a hard constraint)
* S3 -- remains in {{install-helm-chart.sh}} (multi-backend detection is inherently imperative)
* Keycloak -- external by design

h2. Implementation

*PR:* [#120|https://github.com/insights-onprem/cost-onprem-chart/pull/120]

*Database subchart* ({{cost-onprem/charts/cost-onprem-database/}}):
* StatefulSet, Service, ConfigMap (init scripts for multi-DB setup)
* Helm hooks retained for pre-install/pre-upgrade ordering
* Database names shared via {{global.databases}} for parent/subchart consistency

*Cache subchart* ({{cost-onprem/charts/cost-onprem-cache/}}):
* Deployment, Service, PVC with {{helm.sh/resource-policy: keep}}
* Security context with dynamic fsGroup detection for OpenShift

*Parent chart changes:*
* {{Chart.yaml}} -- conditional dependencies
* {{values.yaml}} -- {{database.deploy}} default changed to {{false}}; deployment values moved to {{cost-onprem-database:}} and {{cost-onprem-cache:}} subchart sections; database names moved to {{global.databases}}; {{resources.database}} removed
* {{_helpers.tpl}} -- database name helpers now read from {{global.databases.*}}; removed orphaned helpers

*Scripts & CI:*
* {{install-helm-chart.sh}} -- runs {{helm dependency update}} before install; sets {{database.deploy=true}} for bundled mode
* CI workflows -- lint/release run {{helm dependency update}}
* {{openshift-values.yaml}} -- sets {{database.deploy: true}} for OpenShift deployments

*Documentation:*
* Updated installation, quickstart, disconnected deployment, and configuration docs

h2. Key Design Decisions

||Decision||Rationale||
|Single Helm release|Atomic install/upgrade/rollback, no cross-chart coordination|
|Service names via nameOverride|{{cost-onprem-database}} and {{cost-onprem-valkey}} match parent helper resolution|
|Selector labels use parent chart name|Preserves {{app.kubernetes.io/name: cost-onprem}} for test and monitoring selectors|
|Database names in global.databases|Shared between parent and subchart without duplication|
|database.deploy=false default|Production deployments MUST use enterprise-grade external databases|
|valkey.deploy=true default|Single-instance cache is acceptable; data is ephemeral and recoverable|

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* {{helm lint}} passes
* {{helm template}} produces valid YAML for all four modes (db=true/false x valkey=true/false)
* Service names match parent helper resolution
* DATABASE_SERVICE_HOST and REDIS_HOST resolve correctly in bundled and BYOI modes
* Secret name {{cost-onprem-db-credentials}} consistent across parent and subchart
* E2E tests pass
* oc-mirror image discovery unaffected (FLPATH-3181 compatibility)

h1. insights\-rbac Performance Testing

h2. Context

PR #146 \(\[FLPATH\-4073|[https://github.com/insights\-onprem/cost\-onprem\-chart/pull/146|https://github.com/insights-onprem/cost-onprem-chart/pull/146]\], merged May 10, 2026\) added insights\-rbac as the authorization backend for both Koku and ROS in the on\-prem Helm chart. This introduces a new latency\-additive component in the request path: every Koku API and ROS API request now makes a synchronous HTTP call to insights\-rbac for permission resolution before returning data.

The insights\-rbac deployment consists of:
\* RBAC API \(Gunicorn\) \- handles authorization requests
\* Celery worker \- background processing
\* PostgreSQL database \(costonprem\_rbac\) \- stores roles, groups, policies
\* Valkey \- Celery broker \(shared with existing Valkey instance\)

The performance epic \(FLPATH\-4036\) was created before RBAC was integrated. The test plan must be extended to cover insights\-rbac as a component in the pipeline, particularly its impact on API latency and its behavior under concurrent load.

h2. Scope

h3. 1. RBAC API Latency Baseline

Measure the latency that RBAC adds to every API request:
\* P50/P95/P99 latency of RBAC permission check calls \(Koku to RBAC HTTP round\-trip\)
\* P50/P95/P99 latency of RBAC permission check calls \(ROS API to RBAC HTTP round\-trip\)
\* Compare Koku API response times with and without RBAC enabled \(before/after comparison using the existing baseline data\)
\* Compare ROS API response times with and without RBAC enabled
\* Measure RBAC internal query time \(Django ORM to PostgreSQL for policy resolution\)

h3. 2. RBAC Under Concurrent API Load

Measure RBAC behavior when multiple API consumers are active simultaneously:
\* Concurrent Koku API requests from multiple users with different permission scopes
\* Concurrent ROS API requests from multiple users
\* Mixed workload: API reads during heavy ingestion processing
\* Identify the concurrency level at which RBAC becomes the bottleneck \(Gunicorn worker saturation\)

h3. 3. RBAC with Complex Permission Models

Measure RBAC performance degradation as permission complexity grows:
\* Baseline: single user, single role \(Cost Administrator\)
\* Medium: 10 users, 5 custom roles with namespace\-scoped and cluster\-scoped policies
\* Large: 50 users, 20 custom roles with fine\-grained resource\-level permissions
\* Measure how policy count affects RBAC query time

h3. 4. RBAC Resource Sizing

Determine RBAC resource requirements per deployment tier:
\* CPU and memory consumption under sustained API load
\* Gunicorn worker count tuning \(current default vs optimal for each tier\)
\* RBAC PostgreSQL database size growth with increasing users/roles/policies
\* Valkey memory impact from RBAC Celery tasks and permission caching

h3. 5. RBAC Failure Impact

Characterize system behavior when RBAC is degraded:
\* API behavior when RBAC is slow \(response time > 5s\)
\* API behavior when RBAC is unreachable \(HTTP timeout / connection refused\)
\* Recovery time after RBAC outage \(cold cache rebuild\)
\* Impact on ingestion pipeline \(listener/workers do not call RBAC, so should be unaffected \- verify\)

h3. 6. RBAC Cache Effectiveness

Measure the impact of RBAC permission caching:
\* Cache hit rate under sustained identical\-user API requests
\* Cache invalidation impact when roles/policies are modified
\* Valkey memory consumption from RBAC cache entries at each tier

h2. KPIs to Add

||KPI||Target||Measurement||
|RBAC permission check latency \(Koku\)|< 50ms \(p95\)|Timer on Koku\-to\-RBAC HTTP call|
|RBAC permission check latency \(ROS\)|< 50ms \(p95\)|Timer on ROS\-to\-RBAC HTTP call|
|RBAC API error rate|< 0.1%|HTTP 5xx from RBAC API|
|RBAC Gunicorn worker utilization|< 80%|Active workers / total workers|
|RBAC DB query latency|< 10ms \(p95\)|pg\_stat\_statements on costonprem\_rbac|
|End\-to\-end API latency increase due to RBAC|< 100ms added \(p95\)|Comparison with pre\-RBAC baseline|

h2. Sizing Guide Deliverable

Produce RBAC resource recommendations per deployment tier:

||Tier||API Replicas||Gunicorn Workers||CPU Req/Limit||Memory Req/Limit||Celery Workers||
|Small|1|2|250m/500m|256Mi/512Mi|1|
|Medium|1|4|500m/1|512Mi/1Gi|1|
|Large|2|4|500m/1|512Mi/1Gi|1|
|XL|2|8|1/2|1Gi/2Gi|2|

\(Values are initial estimates, to be validated by testing.\)

h2. Dependencies

* FLPATH\-4061 \(observability stack\) for RBAC metrics collection
* FLPATH\-4063 \(baseline tests\) RBAC latency should be included in API baseline measurements
* FLPATH\-4073 \(insights\-rbac deployment\) merged

h2. Architecture Reference

{code}
User \-> Keycloak JWT \-> Envoy Gateway \-> Koku API / ROS API
                                              | \(HTTP\)
                                         insights\-rbac API <\-> PostgreSQL \(costonprem\_rbac\)
                                              |
                                         Celery Worker <\-> Valkey
{code}

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* RBAC permission check latency is baselined per tier with empirical data
* End\-to\-end API latency impact of RBAC is quantified \(before/after comparison\)
* RBAC behavior under concurrent load is characterized with saturation point identified
* RBAC resource requirements are included in the sizing guide per tier
* RBAC failure modes and recovery characteristics are documented
* Epic's architecture diagram and natural bottlenecks table are updated to include insights\-rbac

items.fromString:
The ros-ocp-backend currently supports OAuth 2.0 authentication through [Kubernetes TokenReview API|https://github.com/redhatinsights/ros-ocp-backend/blob/main/internal/api/middleware/identity.go#L70-L91] but lacks automatic token refresh capabilities. The current implementation validates each request independently using [Kubernetes TokenReview API|https://github.com/redhatinsights/ros-ocp-backend/blob/main/internal/api/middleware/identity.go#L70-L91] and can detect expired tokens through [error handling|https://github.com/redhatinsights/ros-ocp-backend/blob/main/internal/api/middleware/identity.go#L88] but doesn't provide any refresh mechanism.

This approach can be simplified by adding an API gateway that consolidates the authentication for all 3 components and acts as a reverse proxy between the UI and these microservices. The goal of this spike is to study the viability of this approach and document it.

items.toString:
Deploy a metrics collection and reporting pipeline for performance testing. Prometheus scrapes component metrics via ServiceMonitors; exporters provide database and cache visibility; collected data is exported to JSON snapshots and self-contained HTML reports. All outputs are packaged into portable tarballs that can be archived to S3 and consumed by any visualization tool.

h2. What ships

* deploy-observability.sh — deploys celery-exporter, postgres_exporter, valkey-exporter, and Prometheus ServiceMonitors for all cost-onprem components
* collect-metrics.sh — continuous Prometheus metric snapshots during perf runs (configurable interval, 4h max-duration guard)
* generate-perf-run-report.py — self-contained HTML report per run (KPI cards, duration timeline, API latency charts, upload throughput, processing time, time-series)
* generate-perf-matrix-report.py — cross-run HTML comparison matrix (listener CPU × load profile)
* generate-perf-summary.py — flat JSON summary for programmatic consumption
* S3 upload via s3-upload.py — archives tarball of results, metrics, and reports to S3-compatible storage
* Integration flags in deploy-test-cost-onprem.sh: --deploy-observability, --collect-metrics, --upload-metrics

h2. Metrics collected

* Ingress: upload latency, payload sizes, Kafka produce failures
* Kafka: consumer group lag, topic throughput
* Celery: queue depth per queue, task duration, failure rate
* PostgreSQL: query latency p95, active connections, table sizes, WAL write rate, lock contention
* Valkey: memory usage, evictions, connected clients
* ROS: CSV download time, Kruize API latency, aggregation time
* Infrastructure: node CPU, memory, disk I/O, network

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* All exporters deployed and scraping successfully via ServiceMonitors
* pg_stat_statements enabled on PostgreSQL
* Metrics retention set to 30 days (OpenShift user workload monitoring)
* Self-contained HTML report generated per perf run with KPIs, charts, and full results table
* Cross-run comparison matrix report generated across all runs
* All outputs packaged into portable tarballs — no dependency on any specific visualization tool
* S3 upload works with MinIO/Ceph RGW and AWS S3

h2. Design note

The original scope included Grafana dashboards and snapshot automation. This was descoped in favor of self-contained HTML reports and JSON exports. The collected data (Prometheus snapshots, test result JSON, perf-summary.json) is tool-agnostic — consumers can visualize it in Grafana, Jupyter, or any other tool. The deploy script retains a SKIP_GRAFANA flag for optional Grafana deployment but it is not the primary output path.

h3. Upstream insights\-rbac Cache Invalidation — Triage Summary

After triaging the upstream \[insights\-rbac|[https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights\-rbac|https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights-rbac]\] repository, _there is no HTTP API endpoint to flush the authorization cache_. Invalidation is handled automatically via Django signals on normal CRUD, plus programmatic helpers only reachable from Django shell.

h4. insights\-rbac Cache Architecture

The authorization data lives in _Redis DB 1_ via custom cache classes \(\[management/cache.py|[https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights\-rbac/blob/main/rbac/management/cache.py\]|https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights-rbac/blob/main/rbac/management/cache.py]]\), _not_ Django's {{CACHES}} framework \(Redis DB 2\):

||Cache||Key Pattern||TTL||Purpose||
|{{AccessCache}}|{{rbac::policy::tenant={org\_id}::user={uuid}}}|600s|/access/ policy responses per\-principal|
|{{TenantCache}}|{{rbac::tenant::tenant={org\_id}}}|600s|Tenant objects|
|{{PrincipalCache}}|{{rbac::principal::{org\_id}::{username}}}|3600s|Principal DB rows|

{panel:title=Important|borderColor=#DE350B}
The on\-prem docs currently suggest {{cache.clear\(\)}} via Django shell — this only clears _Redis DB 2_ \(Django CACHES\), which does _not_ contain authorization data. To actually flush the authorization cache, you need to target Redis DB 1 via {{AccessCache}}.
{panel}

h4. What exists today

_Signal\-driven invalidation_ works when RBAC changes go through the normal API/ORM \(\[group signals|[https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights\-rbac/blob/main/rbac/management/group/model.py|https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights-rbac/blob/main/rbac/management/group/model.py]\], \[role signals|[https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights\-rbac/blob/main/rbac/management/role/model.py|https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights-rbac/blob/main/rbac/management/role/model.py]\], \[policy signals|[https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights\-rbac/blob/main/rbac/management/policy/model.py\]|https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights-rbac/blob/main/rbac/management/policy/model.py]]\) with {{ACCESS\_CACHE\_CONNECT\_SIGNALS=True}}.

_Programmatic flush_ exists but is not exposed as an API \(\[seeds.py|[https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights\-rbac/blob/main/rbac/management/seeds.py\]\):|https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights-rbac/blob/main/rbac/management/seeds.py]):]
{code}
from management.seeds import purge\_cache\_for\_all\_tenants
purge\_cache\_for\_all\_tenants\(\)

h1. Or per\-tenant:
from management.cache import AccessCache
AccessCache\(""\).delete\_all\_policies\_for\_tenant\(\)
{code}

_No URL routes_ exist for cache invalidation — confirmed by reviewing \[management URLs|[https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights\-rbac/blob/main/rbac/management/urls.py|https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights-rbac/blob/main/rbac/management/urls.py]\], \[internal URLs|[https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights\-rbac/blob/main/rbac/internal/urls.py|https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights-rbac/blob/main/rbac/internal/urls.py]\], and both \[public|[https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights\-rbac/blob/main/docs/source/specs/openapi.json|https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights-rbac/blob/main/docs/source/specs/openapi.json]\] and \[internal|[https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights\-rbac/blob/main/rbac/internal/specs/openapi.json|https://github.com/RedHatInsights/insights-rbac/blob/main/rbac/internal/specs/openapi.json]\] OpenAPI specs.

h4. Full flush requires two targets

||Target||Mechanism||Status||
|Koku RBAC cache \(Valkey, 300s TTL\)|{{POST /masu/invalidate\_cache/}} with {{cache\_name: "rbac"}} \(\[invalidate\_cache.py|[https://github.com/project\-koku/koku/blob/main/koku/masu/api/invalidate\_cache.py\]\)|Already|https://github.com/project-koku/koku/blob/main/koku/masu/api/invalidate_cache.py])|Already] available|
|insights\-rbac AccessCache \(Redis DB 1, 600s TTL\)|No API — requires {{kubectl exec}} or direct Redis access|No endpoint upstream|

h4. Options

h1. _Shell script_ — {{kubectl exec}} into both Koku and RBAC pods \(simplest, no upstream changes\)
h1. _Kubernetes Job_ — runs the Django management commands against both services
h1. _Contribute upstream_ — add {{POST /\_private/api/utils/invalidate\_cache/}} to insights\-rbac, then the on\-prem UX can target both endpoints uniformly
For most use cases, the TTL\-based expiry \(300s Koku / 600s RBAC\) is sufficient. The manual mechanism is for cases where immediate effect is needed after permission changes \(e.g., bootstrap, bulk operations with signals off\).

In order to provide multi tenancy with cost management, we need to ensure that each cost management metrics operator has an associated org_id and account_number in the JWT token retrieved from keycloak. Today that is done via claims in the keycloak client resource. However, the UI interactions with the cluster also need to be able to provide the same org_id and account_name in order to filter the data for each tenant.

The limitation we face is that the information returned from tokenreviewer does not contain that information, even when the cluster is configured to map the keycloak attributes to the "extra" structure in OCP.

This spike aims to clarify why is it not possible and what alternatives are out there to enable the outcome where the REST API calls from the UI can provide these 2 key fields to the backends, such as it is for the cost management metrics operator.

*Fixed version: 0.2.20-rc5*

Add support for Kafka SASL/TLS authentication in the cost-onprem Helm chart for secure connections to enterprise Kafka clusters (AMQ Streams, MSK, Confluent).

h3. Background

PR #99 (FLPATH-2685) added BYOI support for Kafka but scoped it to _PLAINTEXT connections only_. During implementation, we discovered that neither Koku nor ROS applications support Kafka SASL/TLS authentication from environment variables in non-Clowder (on-premise) mode. Chart-level wiring of SASL/TLS values would have no effect without upstream application changes.

h3. Prerequisites (upstream)

Both Koku and ROS need to be updated to read Kafka SASL/TLS configuration from environment variables when running in on-prem mode (non-Clowder):
- Koku: {{KAFKA_SASL_MECHANISM}}, {{KAFKA_SASL_USERNAME}}, {{KAFKA_SASL_PASSWORD}}, {{KAFKA_SECURITY_PROTOCOL}}, {{KAFKA_SSL_CA_LOCATION}}
- ROS: equivalent Go-side configuration via environment variables or config file

Until those upstream changes land, chart-level SASL/TLS support cannot be implemented.

h3. Scope

Once upstream support is available:
- Add {{kafka.sasl.mechanism}}, {{kafka.sasl.existingSecret}}, {{kafka.tls.enabled}}, {{kafka.tls.caCertSecret}} to {{values.yaml}}
- Wire these values into Koku and ROS deployment environment variables via {{_helpers-koku.tpl}} and {{_helpers.tpl}}
- Mount TLS CA certificate from the referenced secret if {{kafka.tls.enabled}}
- Update documentation in {{docs/operations/configuration.md}} (External Kafka section)
- Add E2E test coverage for SASL_SSL connections

h3. Acceptance Criteria

* Chart renders correct SASL/TLS environment variables and volume mounts when configured
* {{helm template}} and {{helm lint}} pass with SASL_SSL configuration
* Documented in the External Kafka section of configuration.md
* Tested against a SASL_SSL-enabled Kafka cluster

items.fromString: CoP - Support External Infrastructure Services (BYOI - Bring Your Own Infrastructure)

items.toString: This issue is related to FLPATH-3318

items.fromString:
The cost-onprem Helm chart currently deploys its own PostgreSQL, Valkey, and 
relies on the install script to deploy Kafka (via Strimzi). These bundled 
deployments are suitable for development, testing, and non-production 
environments but are NOT appropriate for production, where customers will 
typically have their own managed or enterprise-grade infrastructure.

This epic adds first-class support for connecting to externally-managed 
services, allowing customers to "bring their own infrastructure" (BYOI) for:
 - *{*}PostgreSQL{*}* — Use an existing enterprise database (e.g., Crunchy, EDB,
RDS, Azure Database for PostgreSQL). Skip deploying the bundled StatefulSet.
 - *{*}Valkey/Redis{*}* — Use an existing Redis-compatible cache (e.g., Redis
Enterprise, ElastiCache, Azure Cache). Skip deploying the bundled 
Deployment.
 - *{*}Kafka{*}* — Use an existing Kafka broker (e.g., AMQ Streams, Confluent,
MSK) with full SASL/TLS authentication support. Skip Strimzi deployment.
 - *{*}Keycloak{*}* — Connect to a customer-managed Keycloak/RHBK instance with
clear documentation for required realm/client configuration.

Acceptance Criteria (Epic-level):
 - For each service, a boolean flag (e.g., `database.deploy: false`) skips
the internal deployment while still configuring connection strings
 - External connection parameters (host, port, credentials secret, TLS) are
fully configurable via values.yaml
 - Init containers (waitForDb, waitForKafka, etc.) adapt to external
endpoints rather than always targeting internal service names
 - install-helm-chart.sh respects external mode and skips provisioning steps
 - Documentation covers required external service configuration
(schema setup, Keycloak client/realm, Kafka topics, etc.)
 - Existing CI/dev workflow (bundled services) continues to work unchanged

Business Value:
Production deployments require enterprise-grade infrastructure with HA, 
backup, monitoring, and compliance controls that a bundled single-replica 
StatefulSet cannot provide. This epic removes the barrier to production 
adoption by decoupling the application from its infrastructure dependencies.

OpenShift Plus offers ACM/MCM, ODF... see [https://www.redhat.com/en/technologies/cloud-computing/openshift/platform-plus]
 * Modify the helm chart to drop any Kind/vanilla K8s compatibility and tune it for production release. The chart will be then validated by QE before customer deploys it in their environment.
 * Modify the CI/CD in our repos to use openshift-ci and use this helm chart + scripts to deploy keycloak to replace kind as the end to end validation platform.
